headline_en: 'Swarms of missiles and drones fly over our heads'
summary_en: Rashedul Hasan, chief engineer of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (BSC) ship Banglar Joyjatra, describes to Prothom Alo how its 31 Bangladeshi seafarers have lived through the US-Israel war on Iran while stuck in the Persian Gulf. The ship was at Jebel Ali port when the war began, finished unloading on 11 March 2026, tried to leave through the Strait of Hormuz on 12 March and was turned back to the Sharjah anchorage by the UAE coast guard.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (BSC) ship Banglar Joyjatra, with 31 seafarers on board, arrived at Jebel Ali port (UAE) on 27 February 2026 carrying steel coils from Qatar; news of the attack on Iran came at dawn the next day, and the ship had been in the Persian Gulf since before the US-Israel conflict around Iran began.
facts.source_in_article: Rashedul Hasan, chief engineer of Banglar Joyjatra

facts.date: about 1 March 2026 (the night after the war began)
facts.statement: On the night after the war began, at about 1:30 am, a loud blast shook the area around the Banglar Joyjatra at Jebel Ali; the crew started an extra generator, readied the emergency fire pump, gave instructions by walkie-talkie and all took shelter in the ship's most protected room. A control room of a nearby oil depot had been hit and was on fire, with two tugboats trying to put it out.

In the following days the seafarers on the Banglar Joyjatra went to the ship's safe room whenever a warning message arrived on their mobile phones; they saw swarms of missiles and drones from Iran heading towards Dubai, many destroyed in the air and some hitting. A missile also struck one terminal of Jebel Ali port, but no ship was there so major damage was avoided.

BSC managing director Commodore Mahmudul Malek contacted the Banglar Joyjatra repeatedly, and the Ministry of Shipping and the Bangladesh embassy in the UAE checked on the crew regularly; the crew had no opportunity to leave the ship, so they stayed aboard and tightened precautions.

Unloading of the Banglar Joyjatra at Jebel Ali port finished on 11 March 2026 after being disrupted for several days for security reasons; maximum alert was declared on the ship and a separate emergency action plan was made. The ship had been scheduled to go on to Kuwait, but because of the war it was decided to bring it back safely out of the risky area.

On 12 March 2026 the Banglar Joyjatra sailed for the Strait of Hormuz, the only exit from the Persian Gulf. About 66 nautical miles from the entrance it radioed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) authority and got no reply; missiles were seen in the strait area and six ships were attacked while crossing the strait that day. A UAE coast guard patrol then told the ship not to proceed for safety reasons, and it returned to the Sharjah anchorage, where missiles and drones from Iran were again seen passing overhead.

Asked on WhatsApp whether he is still afraid, Rashedul Hasan said the crew has got used to the sound of missiles and drones; at first they were frightened and two seafarers used to cry, but now everyone is braver and is fighting 'a war to keep morale up'.

Rashedul Hasan grew up in Madhabdi, Narsingdi, is a cadet of the 47th batch of Bangladesh Marine Academy, became a chief engineer at BSC in 2024 and is currently the youngest chief engineer in the BSC fleet.

headline_en: One Bangladeshi killed in UAE in Iranian attack
summary_en: The UAE defence ministry said on Sunday 1 March 2026 that Iranian attacks had killed three people in the UAE, one of them a Bangladeshi, and slightly injured 58 people of 15 nationalities including Bangladeshis. A fellow expatriate named the dead Bangladeshi as Saleh Ahmed, a water-supply worker killed in the Ajman area. The ministry also gave counts of missiles and drones detected and intercepted.

facts.statement: Iranian attacks on the United Arab Emirates killed three people, nationals of Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh, according to a UAE defence ministry statement on Sunday 1 March 2026.

The Bangladeshi killed in the Iranian attack on the UAE was named as Saleh Ahmed (also printed Saleh Ahmad); he was killed in the Ajman area and worked in water supply. His old home is in Beanibazar, Sylhet, and he later built a house at Gazitek, Barlekha, Moulvibazar; he leaves a wife, three sons and a daughter.
facts.source_in_article: a fellow expatriate Bangladeshi close to him

facts.statement: 58 people were slightly injured in the Iranian attacks on the UAE: nationals of the Emirates, Egypt, Ethiopia, the Philippines, Pakistan, Iran, India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Azerbaijan, Yemen, Uganda, Eritrea, Lebanon and Afghanistan.

Since Iran's attacks began on Saturday (28 February 2026), the UAE detected 165 ballistic missiles heading towards it, of which 152 were destroyed and 13 fell in the sea; 2 cruise missiles were detected and destroyed; 541 Iranian drones were detected, of which 506 were shot down and 35 crashed inside UAE territory causing loss of life and property.

On the second day of Iranian attacks the UAE air force and air defence destroyed 20 ballistic missiles, 8 of which fell in the sea, plus 2 cruise missiles and 311 drones; 21 drones hit civilian targets.

The UAE defence ministry said debris from intercepted missiles and drones fell in various places and caused light to moderate damage to several civilian installations; it said it is fully prepared for any threat and that the safety of citizens, residents and visitors is its top priority.

The United States and Israel began attacking Iran on the morning of Saturday 28 February 2026, killing Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several top military and civilian officials; in response Iran has been firing missiles and drones at Israel and at US military installations in Middle Eastern countries.

headline_en: Spain to legalise 500,000 migrants: the challenge facing 20,000 Bangladeshis
summary_en: A reader-contributed piece says Spain has announced it will regularise 500,000 undocumented migrants by 31 December 2026, open only to those who entered Spain before 31 December 2025, with applications from April 2026 to 30 June 2026 and no work contract required, only a passport and police clearance. About 20,000 Bangladeshis could benefit, but about 10,000 may miss out because of slow passport and police clearance issuance by Bangladeshi offices. Community leaders urge the government and embassy to speed up, and warn against paying anyone since the final bulletin has not been issued.

facts.statement: The government of Spain has announced an initiative to regularise 500,000 undocumented (irregular) migrants by 31 December 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Spanish government announcement, as reported by the writer

facts.statement: Only those who entered Spain before 31 December 2025 will get the benefit of Spain's 2026 regularisation.
The Spanish government has said the application process for the regularisation will start in April 2026 and the last date will be 30 June 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Spanish government, as reported by the writer

facts.statement: Applicants for Spain's 2026 regularisation will not need any work contract; they only need to properly submit a passport and police clearance certificate.
facts.source_in_article: Spanish government, as reported by the writer

facts.statement: About 20,000 Bangladeshi expatriates in Spain could benefit from the regularisation, but about 10,000 may be deprived of the opportunity because of delays and bureaucratic complications in police clearance and passport issuance.

Bangladeshis in Spain say delays in passport renewal and in issuing police clearance, because the Foreign Ministry and other Bangladeshi government offices work very slowly, are preventing many from applying on time; they call on Bangladeshi offices to speed up passport renewal and police clearance.
facts.source_in_article: expatriate Bangladeshis in Spain, via the writer

facts.statement: Al Mamun, president of Bangladesh Association in Spain, advised people not to make any financial transaction on anyone's inducement, saying the final bulletin (of the regularisation) has not yet come and correct information will be available only then.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's ambassador (to Spain) Masudur Rahman said: 'I have informed all the relevant ministries; all have sincerely promised a solution in the shortest time.'

Fazle Elahi, president of Valiente Bangla, called the regularisation a rare opportunity for Bangladeshis that many may lose unless the government acts fast, and said the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, Foreign Ministry and the Bangladesh embassy in Spain must take it seriously; Khorshed Alam Majumdar, president of Baitul Mukarram Jame Mosque in Madrid, said that if the problems are solved quickly the initiative can open a new horizon for Bangladeshis.
Spain declared general amnesties in 2001 and 2005, but according to the writer a decision to regularise migrants on such easy terms had never been taken before 2026.

headline_en: How much influence do British Bangladeshi voters have on Bangladesh's election
summary_en: An Al Jazeera feature from East London, published in translation ahead of Bangladesh's 12 February 2026 election, looks at expatriate Bangladeshis voting for the first time by postal ballot. Only about 32,000 registered in the UK against roughly 645,000 Bangladeshis in England and Wales, while Saudi Arabia had over 239,000 and Qatar about 76,000 registered. People describe a complicated process (NID card, biometric registration at the High Commission with long queues, then a mobile app), limited publicity and missed deadlines.

facts.statement: For the national election of 12 February 2026, Bangladeshis living abroad got the right to vote for the first time: the Election Commission brought expatriate voters under registration and they vote by postal ballot.

In practice the expatriate vote is only for Bangladeshi citizens who hold a national identity card (NID); many British Bangladeshis, especially those born in the UK, have no citizenship documents and are left out.

To vote from the UK an expatriate needs a national ID card, biometric registration (done at the High Commission, with long queues), and then a further digital step through a mobile app; Khaled Noor said this is quite complicated for many, especially elderly voters.
facts.source_in_article: Khaled Noor, barrister and political analyst, former local councillor, Tower Hamlets

facts.statement: About 32,000 (more than 32,000) Bangladeshi citizens in the UK registered as postal voters, against about 645,000 people in England and Wales who identified as Bangladeshi or British Bangladeshi in the 2021 census.
According to the Election Commission, more than 239,000 expatriate Bangladeshi voters registered in Saudi Arabia and about 76,000 in Qatar, compared with 32,000 in the UK.

About 35 percent of residents of Tower Hamlets alone are Bangladeshi; there are also large numbers of Bangladeshis in Newham and in Barking and Dagenham, and East London is the most densely Bangladeshi area.

Expatriates in East London complained of limited publicity by the authorities; some learned about postal voting late. One person applied for an NID a few days before the deadline but the card arrived after registration closed; an elderly man said 'everything is in the app now, whom do I ask if there is a problem?'. The Bangladesh High Commission in London did not comment when contacted.
facts.source_in_article: expatriates interviewed; Moshahid Ali, editor of weekly Bangla Sanglap

facts.statement: Khaled Noor said people in the UK who are eligible to vote but lack permanent or secure immigration status are wary of speaking about the election because they do not want attention on themselves.

Khaled Noor explained the gap in registration: expatriates in Gulf countries are usually single men whose families are in Bangladesh and who have limited political and social rights there, so they stay tied to Bangladesh, whereas many Bangladeshis in the UK and US live permanently with families, careers and children.

Bangladeshis have lived in Britain for over 100 years; large-scale migration began in the mid-20th century, when in the 1950s and 1960s economic hardship in then East Pakistan and UK labour shortages drew Bengali-speaking men, mostly from Sylhet, to London and Birmingham; the 1971 war brought another wave, followed by family reunion.
Tower Hamlets councillors Sabina Khan and Ohid Ahmed were among several British-Bangladeshi politicians who entered the contest in Bangladesh's election, which caused debate.

headline_en: Remove the disease, not the patient
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial condemns the long-running practice in Middle Eastern countries of quickly sending Bangladeshi workers home without any treatment once they are found HIV-positive. It notes that an HIV-negative certificate is mandatory before going abroad but there is no practical health training, and that returnees get free medicine but very limited counselling, mental health or livelihood support. It calls for mandatory pre-departure health education, raising HIV-based expulsion in bilateral talks, and a separate support structure for returnees.

facts.date: ongoing for many years (as of February 2026)
facts.statement: According to a Prothom Alo report cited in the editorial, Bangladeshi workers found HIV-positive in Middle Eastern countries are hurriedly sent back to Bangladesh without any medical treatment or treatment plan; the practice has gone on for many years.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing Prothom Alo's own report

facts.statement: Many Middle Eastern countries still keep a policy of expelling migrant workers solely because of HIV, although the World Health Organization and the International Labour Organization have repeatedly said that expelling someone only because of HIV is discriminatory.
An HIV-negative certificate is mandatory before a Bangladeshi worker goes abroad, but there is no practical training on reducing risk, safe behaviour or sexual health.

Workers who return to Bangladesh with HIV are given medicine free of charge, but counselling, mental health support and livelihood rehabilitation arrangements are very limited; many fear telling even their families because of sudden loss of work and income and social stigma.

The editorial calls for mandatory health education in simple language for workers before going abroad, for the issue of ending HIV-based expulsion to be raised strongly in bilateral talks with destination countries, and for a separate structure of treatment plus mental health support and rehabilitation for returning affected workers.
The editorial states that HIV does not spread through air or ordinary social contact, and that a person with HIV who is under treatment can live and work normally.

headline_en: Bangladesh determined to build skilled manpower to meet future challenges: Asif Nazrul
summary_en: Speaking at the Global Labour Market Conference in Riyadh on Monday 26 January 2026, Expatriates' Welfare adviser Professor Asif Nazrul said Bangladesh is certifying 60,000 workers a month for the Saudi market under the Skill Verification Programme (SVP) agreement with Saudi Takamol. He also cited the Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Ordinance 2025, ratification of ten ILO fundamental conventions, and the recently signed Bangladesh-Saudi worker recruitment agreement.

facts.statement: As a result of the Skill Verification Programme (SVP) agreement with Saudi Takamol, Bangladesh is now giving skill certificates in various occupations to 60,000 workers every month in line with Saudi labour market demand.
facts.source_in_article: Professor Asif Nazrul, adviser, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, at the Global Labour Market Conference in Riyadh

facts.statement: A worker recruitment agreement between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia was recently signed; Asif Nazrul hoped it will play an important role in safe migration.

The 'Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025' has been issued; according to Asif Nazrul it will make forming trade unions easier, remove gender-based wage discrimination and ban blacklisting of workers.

Asif Nazrul said Bangladesh has ratified ten fundamental ILO conventions (described as within South Asia) and reaffirmed its commitment to fairness, welfare and accountability in the labour market, and that the government has taken various steps to meet growing global demand for skilled manpower.
The Global Labour Market Conference was held in Riyadh for the third time in 2026, attended by the ILO director general (printed as secretary general) and labour ministers of 35 countries in total.

headline_en: National security adviser urges US to ease travel for Bangladeshi businesspeople
summary_en: After the United States added Bangladesh to its visa bond list, National Security Adviser Khalilur Rahman asked US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington DC on Thursday 8 January 2026 to help ease travel for Bangladeshi businesspeople. The US State Department's travel website said on Tuesday (6 January 2026) that nationals of 38 countries including Bangladesh must post a visa bond of up to USD 15,000. The meeting also covered cutting the 20 percent reciprocal tariff.

facts.statement: The US State Department's travel website said on Tuesday (6 January 2026) that nationals of 38 countries including Bangladesh must give a visa bond (security deposit) of up to USD 15,000 when applying to enter the United States; the article gives this as about BDT 1,835,000 at BDT 122.31 per dollar.
facts.source_in_article: US State Department travel website, as reported

facts.statement: The United States has included Bangladesh in its visa bond list.

Bangladesh's National Security Adviser Khalilur Rahman, meeting US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer in Washington DC on the afternoon of Thursday 8 January 2026 local time, said the visa bond will be an obstacle to Bangladeshi businesspeople travelling to the US and asked Greer to play a role from his position in easing their travel; Greer assured cooperation on the matters raised.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Washington DC press release; diplomatic sources

facts.statement: In the same meeting Khalilur Rahman proposed reducing the 20 percent reciprocal tariff currently in force on Bangladesh; Greer promised to consider it positively and to seriously consider reducing or withdrawing the tariff on garments made with US raw materials. Khalilur Rahman also asked for access to DFC funding for Bangladesh's private sector.

headline_en: Wages fall when too many workers go to one country
summary_en: A theoretical research paper presented at a Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) seminar in Agargaon, Dhaka, on Thursday 11 December 2025 argued that when too many workers go to one country an oversupply of labour forms and migrant workers' average wage eventually falls, a risk avoided by sending skilled workers in varied sectors rather than only low-skilled ones. The paper, by Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed of Southern Illinois University, modelled the effects of oil price rises on remittances and migrant workers.

facts.statement: A theoretical research paper presented at a BIDS seminar on 11 December 2025 said that when workers go to a particular country in large numbers, an excess supply of labour is created there and the average wage of migrant workers eventually falls; sending skilled workers in various sectors instead of only low-skilled workers removes this risk.
facts.source_in_article: theoretical research paper by Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed, Southern Illinois University, presented at BIDS

facts.statement: According to the paper, right after oil prices rise, production and working hours rise in the Middle East and other oil-rich countries, earnings of migrant workers in the related sectors increase, existing migrants work more because of higher wages and overtime, and in the first round remittance flows rise significantly.
facts.source_in_article: Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed

facts.statement: The paper shows that when oil prices rise, host (oil-producing) countries gain, with GDP and labour demand rising, while home (labour-exporting) countries like Bangladesh face long-term contraction in production, consumption and spending because costlier imported fuel raises production costs; the living standard of both domestic workers and new aspiring migrants falls.
facts.source_in_article: Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed

facts.statement: The research was titled (in translation) 'The effect of world oil price rises on remittances and migrant workers of small-economy countries'; the seminar was held by BIDS at Agargaon, Dhaka, and chaired by BIDS research director Mohammad Yunus.

named_actors.name: A K M Mahbub Morshed
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Professor of economics who presented the theoretical research at the BIDS seminar.
